Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure, which is defined as one hundred and one point three kilopascals at sea level. This is the reference point used for the Celsius scale.

At higher altitudes the surrounding air pressure falls, so water reaches its boiling point at a lower temperature. Cooking times therefore lengthen noticeably in mountainous regions, and recipes often carry an altitude adjustment note for exactly this reason.

The relationship between pressure and boiling temperature is described by the Clausius Clapeyron relation, which relates the vapour pressure of a liquid to its temperature.
